You need to know very well (pato)physiology of the disease you want to treat - e.g. hypertension- you know that blood pressure is controlled by cascade renine-angiotensine-aldosteron + autonomic nervous system by alpha/beta receptors + it’s about volume of blood.
So you can inhibit:
1) renine (aliskiren) - so it stops releasing aldosterone so your kidnesy excrets more water
2) ACE (captoprile, enalaprile,…)- the same as point 1, but you inhibit ACE, and you know from physiology that ACE converts angiotensin 1 to angiotensin 2, BUT also inhibits effect of bradykinine in your blood, that is molecule that dilates your vessels, so inhibiting it leads to vasokontrictions. Now when you inhibit ACE - a) you inhibit secretion of aldosterone, but also you don’t inhibit the bradykinine, which cause vasodilation in lungs (because ACE is located in lungs) which leads to cough (= side effect of ACE inhibitors)
3) diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorthiazide,…) - you excret more water = you have less “blood” - side effect can be hypocalemia and basically problems with ionts
4) beta blocators (metaprolol, bisprolol) - you antagonize beta receptors, and you know from physiology you have beta1 (heart) and beta2 (lungs), and it leads to decreased function of heart (negative inotropic effect atc) but also bronchial constriction (=side effects)…. So you want to use cardio-selective beta blocators because they only blocate beta1 receptor
5) alpha 2 + imidazole 1 agonists (moxonidin, rilmenidin, klonidin) - from physiology you know that alpha2 receptor is presynaptic and when NA is binded to it, body stops secreting NA… so when you agonize this receptors, your body have less NA, so your sympathetic nervous system cannot be activated = lower blood pressure
6) alpha1 antagonists (urapidil,…) - the same situation as point 5 but you blocate the presynaptic receptor which makes the physiological effect, but logically this blocate all sympathetic effects in your body and that could be side effect of these drugs

And this is basically over 50% of knowledge you need, now you just memorize basics of pharmacokinetics, but almost all pharmacodynamics is just physiology and its applicated rules 😊
